doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Getting through school: Sam Scamacca, music classes and the school big band
summary: Teacher Sam Scamacca excused him from early classes and gym if he got 100 on tests; they ran variety shows with Ronnie Foster and others, and he played Taps.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Did you have trouble getting up in the morning?

Once in a while. She threw water on me a couple of times. She actually did that a couple of times. “You’ve got to get up, you’ve got to go to school.” So then I got a pact with, again, one of the major influences in my life was Sam Scamacca, my high school.

Scamacca. S-C-A-M-A-C-C-A. Sam was cool. Sam was great. And he ended up being the principal there, retired as principal, the whole bit. But when I would go to school Sam basically said okay we’ve got History of Music first period, whatever music course second period and then you’ve got gym. Well he’d give me a note for gym and then let me sleep through my first two classes only under the guise that I would get no less than 100 on the tests. He says, “You know a lot of this. This theory stuff, you know it already. Sedola gave it to you. You already know it.” He said, “And the History of Music you have to read. As long as you get 100 on your test, not 99, 100, that means I can read it all, and then you can sleep through the first periods.” So he would let me stay in the back of the music room and just sleep on a desk.

And he would let me out of gym all the time. He would get me out of gym constantly. As a matter of fact that was the thing, we couldn’t have — and then the other prerequisite with Sam was that I show up on time for the variety shows because we had — well you know Ronnie Foster? Well Ronnie was in the school with us, he was playing in the school. We had Joey Gaeta who is a guitar player that is out in L.A. who has done at least ten albums or so. And Jerry Panzico who has died recently but he was out in L.A. and a great drummer. And so we had a hell of a big band. I mean a really good big band. And Sam is a horn player but he was an aspiring piano player. So he would play piano with us or Ronnie Foster would do it at certain points in time. Matter of fact Ronnie Foster and I used to skip out of school during lunch and go over to my brother’s place, he had a place around the corner, it was like a teen nightclub and there was always a B3 there, and Ronnie and I would go blow for a couple of hours and then we’d come, because I had the key, and then we’d come back to school. It was kind of hip. So Sam, his other prerequisite was that you were on time for all of the things: choir, you had to sing in the choir because he needed in tune voices, and all this kind of stuff. So we did all of it, and he kept us busy and we had the orchestra, I had to play flute or clarinet in the orchestra and then anything else. A couple of times — I remember one variety show where I showed up about 45 minutes late, something like that, and came right in and sat right down and the look he gave me, oh man. He says, “You want what you got? You gotta

pay for it.” He says, “This is the last time.” And that’s the last time I think I was ever late on him. I used to have to play “Taps” because we didn’t have a trumpet player that could play taps, so on Memorial Day when we’d go to the park I’d bring my alto and just hold down low B flat and use the harmonic overtone series. [scats] And I was so egotistical even then, that I told him I would only use a school horn because I didn’t play my horn outside. What if it rained?
